short.headline: India's methane is rising fast, and the source is shifting
short.dek: Cattle still dominate, but coal mines are the fastest-growing slice, and most of the waste problem isn't landfills at all. Two independent estimates now agree almost perfectly.
short.body: India released about 36 million tonnes of methane in 2024, up from 31 million a decade ago. That makes it the world's third-largest emitter, behind China and the US. Agriculture, mainly cattle belching, still accounts for 70% of the total, but its share is shrinking. Fossil-fuel operations, especially coal mining, now produce 12% and are growing fastest. Even the waste slice holds a surprise: it's mostly untreated sewage, not landfills like Ghazipur, roughly six times bigger but too diffuse to ever make a hotspot list. Two independently built global counts, Climate TRACE and Climate Watch, now put India's total methane within 0.4% of each other. The most actionable finding: methane from coal mines and leaks is the one slice we can realistically plug.

macha.heading: Achha, but what's the real story, macha?
macha.body: In plain terms, India is letting out more methane every year, and that matters because methane heats the planet much faster than CO2. Most of it comes from cows and paddy fields, nothing new. But what is new is how fast methane from coal mines, oil wells, and pipelines is rising. These are the leaks we can actually fix: you can't tell a cow to stop burping, but you can seal a mine. Here's the part that will surprise you: even in the waste bucket, it's not the landfills like Ghazipur you hear about, it's untreated sewage flowing through drains, about six times bigger, but nobody can point a camera at a drain the way they can at a dump. The data shows that two independent ways of counting now agree almost perfectly, so we know this is not some model error.
macha.soWhat: Plug the leaks you can reach, coal mines and sewage treatment, not cattle, that is the fastest methane lever.

article.title: How much methane is India actually releasing, and who is responsible for it?
article.standfirst: India's methane emissions are rising, and while agriculture, overwhelmingly cattle, still accounts for the bulk, fossil-fuel operations are the fastest-growing source. Two independent global estimates now agree to within half a per cent, making the shift toward coal mines and leaks the most actionable climate target.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Has India's methane gone up or down over the last decade?

India's methane is rising, not falling. According to Climate TRACE, an independent satellite-informed dataset, all-sector methane emissions climbed from around 31 million tonnes in 2015 to 35.96 million tonnes in 2024. Methane is a potent but short-lived greenhouse gas: over its first 20 years in the air, a tonne of methane traps more than 80 times as much heat as a tonne of CO2, then breaks down in about a decade. That means a rising line of methane has an immediate, outsized effect on warming. The total warming punch, measured as 20-year CO2-equivalent, went from about 4.9 billion tonnes in 2015 to 6.27 billion tonnes in 2024, driven largely by methane. So the trend is not just academic; it is about how fast the planet heats this decade.

## Where does India rank among the world's methane emitters?

India ranked third in 2023, releasing 35.27 million tonnes of methane. China was far ahead at 83.02 million tonnes, and the United States second at 38.31 million tonnes. After India came Russia at 21.06 million, Brazil at 19.42 million, and Indonesia at 14.93 million. This is a snapshot of annual flows, not a scorecard of historical responsibility or per-person amounts. India's position reflects its vast agriculture and coal production, not its per-capita emissions. Most reputable inventories put India in the top three, though the exact rank can shift by a spot depending on revisions and which inventory is used. The country's methane output is about 9% of the global total.

## Which sector releases the most methane in India?

Agriculture. In 2024, it accounted for 69.9% of India's methane, or 25.14 million tonnes. Within that, cattle digestion, called enteric fermentation, made up 78.4%, about 19.7 million tonnes, while rice cultivation contributed 17.3%, or 4.3 million tonnes. That means cattle belch out more than four times as much methane as flooded rice paddies. Agriculture's dominance is enormous, but its share has been slipping: it was 75% in 2015. Still, absolute emissions have grown, from 23.26 million tonnes in 2015 to 25.14 million in 2024, because the overall pie is expanding. So even as its relative weight declines, farming remains the elephant in the room.

## Which sector's methane share is growing fastest?

Fossil-fuel operations. Their share rose from 8.3% in 2015 to 11.9% in 2024, a climb of more than 40% in share. In absolute terms, methane from coal mines, oil wells, and gas pipelines jumped from 2.56 million tonnes to 4.28 million tonnes. Waste also crept up, from 11.9% to 13.7%. The shift matters because fugitive methane, leaks from extraction and transport, is the most actionable category: you can seal a leaking coal seam or capture gas before it escapes. Agriculture, with its millions of individual cattle and paddy fields, is much harder to tighten. The trend line shows that fossil fuel methane is not just growing; it is accelerating relative to the rest.

## Who are the biggest named methane polluters in India?

A list of 15 top point sources reads like a roll call of Coal India's opencast mines. The largest is the Cambay onshore oil and gas region at 12.17 million tonnes CO2-equivalent (100-year), followed by Assam onshore at 9.09 million tonnes. Then come the mines: Dipka at 3.58 million, Nigahi and Dudhichua at 2.86 million each, Gevra at 2.62 million, Kusmunda at 2.21 million, Lingaraj at 2.11 million, Amlohri at 1.92 million, and Block II (BOCP) at 1.85 million. Most belong to subsidiaries like South Eastern Coalfields, Northern Coalfields, and Mahanadi Coalfields. The ranking uses CO2e, not pure methane, because it blends in some CO2 from associated sources; refineries are excluded because their emissions are mostly combustion CO2, not methane leaks. But the picture is clear: named methane hotspots in India are overwhelmingly coal mines, not landfills or gas plants.

## Wait, isn't waste methane mostly from landfills?

No. In the waste sector, domestic wastewater, untreated or partly treated sewage, accounts for 81.5% of methane, or 4.02 million tonnes, while solid waste disposal (landfills and dumps) contributes only 13.6%, about 670,000 tonnes. That is a roughly 6-to-1 split. This has been true consistently from 2015 onward. The reason landfills dominate headlines is simple: they are big, smelly, and concentrated. A single landfill like Ghazipur is a named point source you can photograph, while domestic wastewater methane wafts up from thousands of towns' drains, open sewers, and half-functioning treatment plants. It is diffuse, so it rarely makes top-10 lists. But from a climate standpoint, it is the far larger problem.

## So which landfills are the worst?

Even though landfills are not the waste sector's main event, some are individually huge. The top named waste sources in Climate TRACE's data include Majura Taluka in Surat at about 581,000 tonnes CO2e, Pirana in Ahmedabad at about 552,000, Ghazipur in Delhi at about 486,000, Perugundi at about 460,000, Kodungaiyur in Chennai at about 362,000, Bhalaswa at about 331,000, and Dhapa in Kolkata at about 320,000. The list also features Bandra, but it is a wastewater treatment site, not a landfill. These figures underscore that while diffuse sewage dominates nationally, a few city landfills remain methane mega-sources. Their emissions are both a climate concern and a local health hazard, as surrounding communities know firsthand.

## Can we trust these numbers? What does a second estimate say?

Two independently built global databases now point to nearly the same total. Climate TRACE, which uses satellite observations and bottom-up per-source modelling, estimated India's methane at 31 million tonnes in 2015 and 35.27 million in 2023. Climate Watch, a gap-filled reconstruction often used to complete official inventories, put the numbers at 33.21 and 35.13 million tonnes for the same years. The gap shrank from -2.21 million tonnes (-6.7%) to just 0.14 million tonnes (+0.4%). When two methods that started 7% apart converge to within half a per cent, it does not prove correctness, but it makes both more credible. The increase in Climate TRACE's estimates in later years drove the convergence, suggesting satellite-informed data is catching up with the modelled average.

## Do the two estimates agree on agriculture?

Yes, they track closely. Climate TRACE consistently reports a bit more agricultural methane: 23.26 million tonnes in 2015 versus Climate Watch's 21.97 million (a 5.8% gap), and 25.1 million in 2023 versus 23.53 million (6.7% gap). The offset of roughly 1.5 million tonnes persists across years, but the trends move in lockstep. This likely reflects slightly different assumptions about how much methane each cow or each hectare of paddy emits, the emission factors, rather than any disagreement about the activity data itself. Since agriculture is the largest sector, this steady, parallel offset gives confidence that the overall shape and size of India's farm methane are well understood.

## What about fossil-fuel methane?

This is where the convergence is most dramatic. In 2015, Climate TRACE estimated fossil-fuel operations at 2.56 million tonnes of methane, while Climate Watch's fugitive emissions estimate was 3.48 million tonnes, a gap of -26.5%. By 2023, the numbers had practically merged: 3.72 million tonnes from Climate TRACE, 3.7 million from Climate Watch, a difference of just 0.5%. That narrowing likely reflects improvements in satellite detection of leaks from coal mines and oil and gas fields, as well as methodological updates. Because fossil fuel methane is the fastest-growing slice, this agreement matters: it suggests we now have a reliable handle on the very emissions that are most feasible to cut.

## How to read these numbers

Climate TRACE is a satellite-informed inventory that builds up estimates from individual sources, not a direct measurement of the atmosphere. Climate Watch fills the gaps between official reports with modelled data. Asset-level rankings use 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP100) in CO2e, mixing methane's warming effect with a small portion of CO2; they are not pure methane tonnages. India's own official inventories are in its Biennial Update Reports (BUR-3, covering 2016 data, submitted in 2021; BUR-4, covering 2020, submitted in December 2024). These are snapshots years apart, not a continuous time series, a structural feature of how developing countries report under the UNFCCC, not an attempt to hide anything. One honest gap remains: there is no second independent estimate for India's waste sector methane to cross-check the domestic-wastewater-versus-landfills split. That finding rests on Climate TRACE's subsector modelling alone, and the official anchor is a single snapshot from 2020.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A powerful greenhouse gas that traps over 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years but breaks down in about a decade. Think of it like a short, intense fever — it does its damage quickly and then dissipates.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Cutting methane now gives the fastest near-term cooling effect, so knowing who emits it shapes climate strategy.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: An independently built global emissions database that uses satellite observations, activity data, and modelling to estimate emissions for every country and major facility. It is not an official government report.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: This article is largely built on Climate TRACE data, so understanding its independent, satellite-informed nature is essential.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Another global database that compiles and models emissions data, often used to fill gaps between countries' official submissions. It uses a different methodology than Climate TRACE.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: We compare Climate TRACE to Climate Watch to see if the numbers are trustworthy.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A way to express the warming effect of different greenhouse gases in a single number, by converting them to the equivalent amount of CO2. The '100yr' or '20yr' indicates the time horizon used.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The named point sources are given in CO2e (100yr), not raw methane, so comparisons with sector CH4 totals must be careful.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The digestive process in cattle (and other ruminants) where microbes break down food and produce methane, which the animal burps out. It is the main way livestock add methane to the atmosphere.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It makes up about 78% of India's agriculture methane, so 'livestock methane' largely means cattle burps.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Methane (or other gases) that escape during fossil fuel extraction, processing, and transport — like leaks from coal mines, oil wells, or pipelines. They are not from burning the fuel, but from handling it.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Most of India's fossil-fuel methane is fugitive, especially from coal mining. It is the type that can be captured if leaks are plugged.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A single, identifiable location that emits pollution — like a specific coal mine, landfill, or factory. It contrasts with 'diffuse' sources like sewage from thousands of small outfalls.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The article names specific point sources from Climate TRACE's asset-level data, but the waste sector's biggest source (domestic wastewater) is diffuse and has no single point source.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A report that developing countries like India submit to the UN climate body every two years (in theory), containing an inventory of greenhouse gas emissions. They are often published with a multi-year delay.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's official numbers are in its BURs, but they are snapshots from years ago. That is why independent estimates are useful to fill the gap.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A metric that compares the heat trapped by a gas over 100 years to the heat trapped by the same amount of CO2. Methane's GWP100 is about 28, meaning it traps 28 times more heat over a century.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Asset-level data uses GWP100 to convert everything to CO2e, so the rankings mix warming effects, not just methane tonnage.

chartExplainers.takeaway: India's all-sector methane emissions climbed from roughly 31 million tonnes in 2015 to 35.96 million tonnes in 2024.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart plots India's annual methane emissions in tonnes of CH4 from 2015 through 2024. The line rises steadily, showing a clear upward trend. Methane is a potent short-lived gas; it warms the planet over 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years, so this increase has an immediate climate impact. The data comes from Climate TRACE, a satellite-informed inventory that builds estimates from activity data and emission factors, not direct atmospheric sampling. chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Before any breakdown, the headline trend answers whether India's methane problem is getting better or worse.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line shows annual CH4 in tonnes; focus on the upward slope from 2015 to 2024.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't confuse the gradual rise with a plateau; the increase is steady and significant in climate terms because methane is so potent.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a phone, the line chart should have sparse ticks and a clear y-axis label to keep it readable.

chartExplainers.title: India is the world's third-biggest methane emitter
chartExplainers.takeaway: India released 35.27 million tonnes of methane in 2023, ranking third behind China (83.02 million tonnes) and the United States (38.31 million tonnes).
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal bar chart compares methane emissions for the top emitting countries in 2023. China dominates at 83 million tonnes, more than double India's output. The US edges out India by about 3 million tonnes. Russia, Brazil, and Indonesia follow with significantly lower numbers. The chart uses a single year's snapshot from one estimate (Climate TRACE), so it reflects current annual flows, not historical responsibility or per-capita contributions. India's rank underlines the scale of its methane challenge, driven by agriculture and growing fossil activity.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Scale means little without company: where does India sit next to the other big emitters?
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars show total methane tonnes for the top few countries in 2023; India's bar is third behind China and the US, and about half of China's.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is a snapshot of annual flows, not past contributions or per-person amounts; India's ranking does not reflect historical responsibility.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use horizontal bars with country labels to make scanning easy on a small screen.

chartExplainers.title: Livestock and rice still dominate, but their share is shrinking
chartExplainers.takeaway: Agriculture accounted for 69.9% of India's methane in 2024, with cattle alone responsible for 78.4% of that slice.
chartExplainers.detail: This composition chart shows the sector breakdown of India's methane for the latest year (2024). The dominant block is agriculture, at 69.9%. Within agriculture, enteric fermentation (cattle digestion) makes up 19.7 million tonnes, or 78.4% of the sector, while rice cultivation contributes only 4.3 million tonnes (17.3%). Waste (13.7%) and fossil-fuel operations (11.9%) are smaller but growing. This snapshot reveals that while 'agriculture' often conjures an image of paddy fields, it is overwhelmingly cattle burps that matter. The composition underscores why cutting methane from farming is so hard: millions of individual animals, not point sources.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Solutions depend on the source: a cattle-and-rice problem needs different fixes than a coal-mine or landfill problem. The hidden dominance of cattle over rice is a important nuance.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A stacked bar or pie chart shows sector shares for the latest year. Note that within the agriculture slice, cattle (enteric fermentation) far outweighs rice, as shown by a separate inset or annotation.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume 'agriculture' means an even split between livestock and rice; it's mostly cattle burps.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use clear colour coding and large percentage labels to convey the shares at a glance.

chartExplainers.title: Fossil-fuel methane's share has grown fastest
chartExplainers.takeaway: Fossil-fuel operations' share of India's methane rose from 8.3% in 2015 to 11.9% in 2024, a relative increase of over 40%.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the percentage share of each sector over 2015-2024. Agriculture's share declined from 75% to 69.9%, while fossil fuel operations climbed steadily. Waste also edged up from 11.9% to 13.7%. The absolute tonnage of fossil-fuel methane grew from 2.56 to 4.28 million tonnes. This shift is important because fugitive emissions from coal mines and oil/gas systems are point-source concentrated, making them more feasible to capture than diffuse agricultural methane. The chart shows that while agriculture remains the largest source, the pace of change is in the fossil sector.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A composition snapshot hides which slice is actually growing fastest, and it isn't agriculture. The trend line shows the shift.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart showing percentage shares over time. Watch the fossil-fuel line rise while agriculture gradually dips.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Agriculture's declining share does not mean its absolute emissions are falling; it's that fossil-fuel emissions grew faster.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the lines distinct with clear labels and a straightforward y-axis (0-80% range) for easy reading.

chartExplainers.title: India's named methane hotspots are almost all coal mines
chartExplainers.takeaway: The top 15 point sources are overwhelmingly opencast coal mines run by Coal India subsidiaries, with two large oil and gas regions leading.
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal bar chart ranks the 15 largest named point sources by CO2e (100-year). The biggest are the Cambay onshore oil and gas region (12.17 million tonnes CO2e) and Assam onshore (9.09 million). The rest are coal mines: Dipka (3.58 million), Nigahi, Dudhichua, Gevra, Kusmunda, Lingaraj, Amlohri, and Block II (BOCP), among others. These mines are operated by subsidiaries like South Eastern Coalfields and Northern Coalfields. The ranking uses a blended CO2e metric, not pure methane, so it reflects total warming impact (including any associated CO2). Refineries were excluded because their emissions are mostly combustion CO2. The visual makes clear that coal mining, not landfills, dominates India's methane point-source landscape.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Sector totals are abstract; naming the actual sites makes the story concrete. Coal mines dominate, not landfills or gas fields.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A horizontal bar chart ranking 15 point sources by CO2e. Top entries include coal mines (Dipka, Nigahi, Dudhichua, Gevra, etc.) and two oil/gas regions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are CO2e values, not pure methane; avoid direct comparison with sector CH4 totals. Also, refineries are excluded because their emissions are mainly CO2.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Long site names require horizontal bars with sufficient padding; consider abbreviating or stacking labels if needed.

chartExplainers.title: Landfills aren't where most of India's waste methane comes from
chartExplainers.takeaway: Domestic wastewater contributes 81.5% of waste-sector methane, versus 13.6% from solid waste disposal, a roughly 6-to-1 split.
chartExplainers.detail: This composition chart splits India's 4.94 million tonnes of waste methane in 2024 into domestic wastewater (4.02 million tonnes) and solid waste disposal (about 670,000 tonnes). The dominance of wastewater is striking and steady over the decade. It occurs because untreated or partially treated sewage releases large amounts of methane as it decomposes, and this source is diffuse across thousands of towns and cities. Landfills, while visually dramatic, represent a smaller fraction. The chart corrects the intuitive impression that waste methane is primarily a landfill problem.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The named-landfills chart that follows could leave the impression that landfills are the waste sector's main event, the subsector split says otherwise.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A composition stack or share strip for 2024 shows domestic wastewater at over 80% and solid waste disposal under 14%. The absolute tonnes are shown.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't conclude landfills are unimportant; they are still large point sources, but the diffuse wastewater problem is the bigger climate factor.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a simple stacked bar with large percentage labels for the two main categories.

chartExplainers.title: The landfills you'd actually recognise
chartExplainers.takeaway: The top named waste sources include Majura Taluka (Surat), Pirana (Ahmedabad), and Ghazipur (Delhi), each releasing over 480,000 tonnes CO2e.
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal bar chart lists the top 10 named landfill and wastewater sites by CO2e. Majura Taluka tops at about 581,000 tonnes, followed by Pirana at about 552,000 and Ghazipur at about 486,000. Others include Perugundi, Kodungaiyur, Bhalaswa, and Dhapa. Bandra appears, but it is a wastewater treatment site, not a landfill. These sites are city landmarks, often in the news for fires and health hazards. Their emissions are dwarfed by the diffuse domestic wastewater problem highlighted in the previous chart, but they remain concentrated hotspots with local air quality impacts.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Landfills rarely crack a combined ranking against coal mines by raw tonnage, but Ghazipur and Pirana are the household names of India's waste-methane problem and deserve their own frame.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A horizontal bar chart of the top 10 waste sites, with names like Majura Taluka (Surat), Pirana, Ghazipur. Note the unit is CO2e, not CH4.

chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use familiar city names as labels to help readers connect; keep bars scaled to the largest value.

chartExplainers.title: Two different ways of counting India's methane now roughly agree
chartExplainers.takeaway: Climate TRACE and Climate Watch estimates for India's total methane converged from a 6.7% gap in 2015 to just 0.4% in 2023.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart overlays two independent global estimates: Climate TRACE (satellite-informed) and Climate Watch (gap-filled model). In 2015, they differed by 2.21 million tonnes (Climate TRACE lower); by 2023, the difference was only 0.14 million tonnes. The convergence is driven by Climate TRACE's estimates rising faster, perhaps reflecting improved detection. At 35 million tonnes total, a 0.4% gap is negligible. This agreement boosts confidence that India's methane quantity is reasonably well quantified, despite the methods' differences.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: One estimate alone invites doubt. Does a second, differently-built one land anywhere close? Convergence shows both are credible.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines (Climate TRACE and Climate Watch) over time. They start about 2 million tonnes apart in 2015 and nearly overlap by 2023.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The gap is shown in million tonnes; a 0.14 million tonne gap in 2023 is very small relative to 35 million tonnes total, about 0.4%.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Two lines with distinct colours and a simple legend; a narrow chart height works well here.

chartExplainers.title: Agriculture methane: the two estimates track closely
chartExplainers.takeaway: Climate TRACE's agriculture methane is consistently about 1.5 million tonnes higher than Climate Watch's, with parallel trends.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart compares the two estimates for agriculture-only methane. Climate TRACE runs from 23.26 to 25.1 million tonnes (2015-2023), while Climate Watch goes from 21.97 to 23.53 million tonnes. The gap hovers around 5-7%. Both lines rise together, indicating that the underlying activity data (livestock numbers, rice acreage) and trends are captured similarly. The offset likely arises from different emission factors, how much methane each cow or paddy field is assumed to produce. This consistency is reassuring for the largest sector.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Agriculture is the biggest slice, so it is the most important sector to see cross-checked.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines showing agriculture-only methane. Climate TRACE is consistently higher by about 1.5 million tonnes, but the trends parallel each other.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The persistent offset does not mean one is wrong; it likely reflects different assumptions about emission factors. The parallel trend is reassuring.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a clean line chart with consistent y-axis scaling and clear annotation of the gap.

chartExplainers.title: Fossil-fuel methane: the smallest gap of all
chartExplainers.takeaway: The two estimates for fossil-fuel methane nearly merged by 2023, from a massive -26.5% gap in 2015 to a 0.5% gap.
chartExplainers.detail: This dramatic line chart shows Climate TRACE's fossil-fuel operations methane (2.56 to 3.72 million tonnes) versus Climate Watch's fugitive emissions (3.48 to 3.7 million tonnes). In 2015, Climate TRACE was 0.92 million tonnes lower. That gap shrank to just 0.02 million tonnes by 2023. The convergence likely reflects methodological improvements and better satellite detection of leaks. Since fossil fuel methane is the fastest-growing and most actionable portion, this near-perfect agreement is practically important: it suggests the numbers are now reliable enough to underpin mitigation efforts.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Coal-mine and oil-and-gas fugitive methane is the sector growing fastest in share, worth checking it isn't an artifact of one model.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India's methane emissions are rising, and while agriculture (overwhelmingly cattle) still accounts for the bulk, fossil-fuel operations—coal mining above all—are the fastest-growing source; two independent estimates now agree to within half a per cent after starting 7% apart, making the shift away from agriculture the most actionable finding.
requiredConcepts: Scale and trend: Climate TRACE shows India's all-sector methane rose from roughly 31 million tonnes in 2015 to about 35.96 million tonnes by 2024.
World ranking: India is the third-largest methane emitter in 2023, behind China and the United States.
Methane's potency: Methane traps far more heat per tonne than CO2 over the first two decades, then breaks down in about a decade, making near-term cuts a powerful lever for slowing warming now.

Sector composition and shift: Agriculture (cattle digestion and rice paddies) dominates but its share slipped from 75% in 2015 to 69.9% in 2024. Fossil-fuel operations grew from 8.3% to 11.9% of the total, waste from 11.9% to 13.7%.
Agriculture subsector split: Enteric fermentation from cattle accounts for roughly 78.4% of agriculture methane (19.7 million tonnes) versus 17.3% from rice cultivation (4.3 million tonnes) in 2024.
Fossil-fuel subsector split: Coal mining is the largest fossil-fuel methane source, about 1.75 million tonnes, compared to oil and gas at 1.33 million tonnes in 2024.

Named point sources: The top methane-relevant point sources are overwhelmingly opencast coal mines run by Coal India subsidiaries, plus two large onshore oil-and-gas regions; data is in CO2e, not pure CH4.
Waste composition: Domestic wastewater accounts for 81.5% of waste-sector methane in 2024, versus 13.6% from solid waste disposal (landfills), a roughly 6-to-1 split.

Reconciliation of two estimates: Climate TRACE and Climate Watch, independently built, converged from a 6.7% gap in 2015 to just 0.4% in 2023 for total methane, with close agreement in agriculture and fossil-fuel operations.

Methodology honesty: Climate TRACE uses satellite-informed bottom-up modelling, Climate Watch is a gap-filled modelled reconstruction; official Biennial Update Reports are sparse and lagged; no independent series exists for waste.

chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume 'agriculture' means an even split between livestock and rice; it's mostly cattle burps.

chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Agriculture's declining share does not mean its absolute emissions are falling; it's that fossil-fuel emissions grew faster.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A powerful greenhouse gas that traps over 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years but breaks down in about a decade. Think of it like a short, intense fever—it does its damage quickly and then dissipates.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Cutting methane now gives the fastest near-term cooling effect, so knowing who emits it shapes climate strategy.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: An independently built global emissions database that uses satellite observations, activity data, and modelling to estimate emissions for every country and major facility. It is not an official government report.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: This article is largely built on Climate TRACE data, so understanding its independent, satellite-informed nature is essential.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Another global database that compiles and models emissions data, often used to fill gaps between countries' official submissions. It uses a different methodology than Climate TRACE.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: We compare Climate TRACE to Climate Watch to see if the numbers are trustworthy.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A way to express the warming effect of different greenhouse gases in a single number, by converting them to the equivalent amount of CO2. The '100yr' or '20yr' indicates the time horizon used.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The named point sources are given in CO2e (100yr), not raw methane, so comparisons with sector CH4 totals must be careful.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The digestive process in cattle (and other ruminants) where microbes break down food and produce methane, which the animal burps out. It's the main way livestock add methane to the atmosphere.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It makes up about 78% of India's agriculture methane, so 'livestock methane' largely means cattle burps.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Methane (or other gases) that escape during fossil fuel extraction, processing, and transport—like leaks from coal mines, oil wells, or pipelines. They are not from burning the fuel, but from handling it.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Most of India's fossil-fuel methane is fugitive, especially from coal mining. It's the type that can be captured if leaks are plugged.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A single, identifiable location that emits pollution—like a specific coal mine, landfill, or factory. It contrasts with 'diffuse' sources like sewage from thousands of small outfalls.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The article names specific point sources from Climate TRACE's asset-level data, but the waste sector's biggest source (domestic wastewater) is diffuse and has no single point source.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A report that developing countries like India submit to the UN climate body every two years (in theory), containing an inventory of greenhouse gas emissions. They are often published with a multi-year delay.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's official numbers are in its BURs, but they are snapshots from years ago. That's why independent estimates are useful to fill the gap.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A metric that compares the heat trapped by a gas over 100 years to the heat trapped by the same amount of CO2. Methane's GWP100 is about 28, meaning it traps 28 times more heat over a century.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Asset-level data uses GWP100 to convert everything to CO2e, so the rankings mix warming effects, not just methane tonnage.

plannedCharts.title: India's methane is rising, not falling
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE · India's all-sector methane emissions · 2015-2024
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Before any breakdown, the headline trend: is India's methane going up or down.

plannedCharts.title: India is the world's third-biggest methane emitter
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE · methane emissions, selected countries · 2023
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Scale means little without company: where does India actually sit next to the other big emitters.

plannedCharts.title: Livestock and rice still dominate, but their share is shrinking
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE · India's methane by sector, latest year
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Solutions depend on the source: a cattle-and-rice problem needs different fixes than a coal-mine or landfill problem.

plannedCharts.title: Fossil-fuel methane's share has grown fastest
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE · sector shares of India's methane · 2015-2024
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A composition snapshot hides which slice is actually growing fastest - and it isn't agriculture.

plannedCharts.title: India's named methane hotspots are almost all coal mines
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE asset-level data · top 15 named waste and fossil-fuel point sources
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Sector totals are abstract; naming the actual sites makes the story concrete.

plannedCharts.title: Landfills aren't where most of India's waste methane comes from
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE · India's waste-sector methane by subsector, latest year
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The named-landfills chart that follows could leave the impression that landfills are the waste sector's main event - the subsector split says otherwise.

plannedCharts.title: The landfills you'd actually recognise
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE asset-level data · top 10 named landfill and wastewater sites
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Landfills rarely crack a combined ranking against coal mines by raw tonnage, but Ghazipur and Pirana are the household names of India's waste-methane problem and deserve their own frame - even though the previous chart shows they are not the majority source.

plannedCharts.title: Two different ways of counting India's methane now roughly agree
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE (satellite-based) vs. Climate Watch (modelled reconstruction) · India, all sectors
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: One estimate alone invites doubt. Does a second, differently-built one land anywhere close?

plannedCharts.title: Agriculture methane: the two estimates track closely
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE vs. Climate Watch · India agriculture-sector methane
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Agriculture is the biggest slice, so it is the most important sector to see cross-checked.

plannedCharts.title: Fossil-fuel methane: the smallest gap of all
plannedCharts.subtitle: Climate TRACE (fossil-fuel operations) vs. Climate Watch (fugitive emissions) · India
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Coal-mine and oil-and-gas fugitive methane is the sector growing fastest in share (Act 2) - worth checking it isn't an artifact of one model.
